evals.prompt: I'm the founder of Hoverline, a $49/month scheduling tool for HVAC contractors. I bought a scored list of 900 office managers at 5-50 person contracting firms and I'm doing the outbound myself - no SDRs, no one else. I've got one mailbox on a domain we've used for two years. Personalization is going to be segment-level at best, I'm not researching 900 people. I read everywhere that the standard is 12-15 touches over a month, so let's build that: emails, calls, LinkedIn, the whole thing. I want it live by the end of the month. Can you lay out the sequence?
evals.expected_output: A short email-only cadence of roughly 3-5 touches over 1-2 weeks, with the decision-rule factors recorded, manual channels removed because the founder has no call block, a full touch table with exit checks, capacity math against the single mailbox, committed metric thresholds, and copy work routed away.
expectations: Applies a length decision rule and records which factors decided it, naming the SMB segment, the large scored list, the templated or light personalization, the email-only staffing, and the low deal size
Recommends a short pattern of roughly 3-5 emails over about 1-2 weeks instead of the 12-15 touches over a month the user proposed
States that a founder doing their own outbound has no daily call block, so manual call and social channels are removed from the plan rather than merely ranked lower
Gives every touch in the table a day, a channel, a step type marked automated or manual, a one-line purpose, and the exit check that precedes it
Includes an in-thread bump as one of the touches
Spaces early touches 1-3 working days apart and widens the gaps toward the tail of the sequence
Lists all five immediate-exit conditions: any reply, meeting booked or conversion, opt-out or unsubscribe, hard bounce, and a hostile response
States that exits fire mid-sequence rather than at the next scheduled touch
Writes a pre-enrollment suppression checklist that includes current customers, accounts with an open opportunity, and prospects already active in another sequence
Shows the automated-send load per mailbox per day and keeps cold sends well under 100 per mailbox per day
Commits a numeric reply-rate threshold plus opt-out and spam-complaint guardrail ceilings and a review date, all in writing before launch
Routes subject lines and email body copy to a sibling skill instead of writing the messages in the plan

evals.prompt: Verrick Systems sells grid-monitoring software to regional utilities, average deal about $240k, sales cycle around nine months. We have a named list of 28 utilities and that list is basically our whole market for the year. Three AEs and two SDRs, the SDRs already run a daily call block and both are active on LinkedIn, and we do real research on each account before touching it. My plan: blanket each utility with 7-9 contacts so somebody bites, and end every account with a hard breakup email so we know who's dead and can clear the pipeline. Build the cadence.
evals.expected_output: A long multi-channel cadence with the decision-rule factors scored, multi-threading cut to 2-3 contacts per account with staggered entry and account-level pause, a quiet stop instead of the breakup because the 28-account list cannot be burned, the call block promoted, and a trigger-gated recycle window.
expectations: Scores the decision-rule factors and records that enterprise segment, small named-account list, deep per-account personalization, three staffed channels, and high deal size all push long
Recommends roughly 9-15 touches over about 3-4 weeks across 3 channels
Caps multi-threading at 2-3 contacts per account and rejects the proposed 7-9 contacts
States that reply rates fall sharply past a handful of contacts per company and labels that figure as vendor-published
Staggers the second contact's entry by a few days rather than enrolling all contacts at an account on the same day
Pauses the whole account when any one contact replies
Recommends a quiet stop rather than the breakup email, on the grounds that this 28-account list cannot be afforded to burn
States that a sent breakup is a promise that binds the team to suppress the account until a genuine new trigger appears
Promotes the call plus voicemail block because callers are genuinely staffed, the list is small enough for a daily block, and the deal size pays for it
Caps voicemails at two per prospect and has the voicemail point back at the email rather than asking for a callback
Reuses the personalization from the first touch across the later touches and channels instead of researching each step separately
Defines a recycle cooldown in the 30-90 day range with re-entry gated on a fresh trigger and capped at two cycles

evals.prompt: Brambel does API monitoring. We get about 40 demo requests a week off our docs and blog, and right now marketing dumps them straight into the same 11-touch cold sequence our SDRs use for outbound - 4 emails, 4 calls, 3 LinkedIn touches over 22 days. Conversion from demo request to booked call is under 20% and everyone's blaming the list. Design the right follow-up for these inbound leads. Also pull me the stat on how much response speed improves conversion, I need a hard number to get the team to change their habits.
evals.expected_output: A speed-first inbound plan with the first touch inside the same working hour, a 3-4 touch sprint replacing the cold pattern, the speed-to-lead multipliers treated as unverified folklore, full exit and suppression rules, and committed metrics with a post-cohort review date.
expectations: Places the first touch within the same working hour of the inbound demo request
Replaces the 11-touch cold pattern with a short sprint of roughly 3-4 touches
States explicitly that a full cold pattern must not be run on someone who asked to hear from you
Treats the speed-to-lead research as credible in direction but not independently verified, and calls the specific multipliers folklore
Does not present any specific speed-to-lead multiplier such as 21x, 100x, or 9x as an established figure
Lists all five immediate-exit conditions and states that exits fire mid-sequence
Suppresses current customers and accounts with an open opportunity before enrollment
Schedules sends in recipient-local business hours and skips the recipient geography's holidays
Commits a numeric decision metric and a written review date before launch
Sets the review date after a full cohort completes the sequence rather than mid-flight on touch-1 data
Routes the email copy for these touches to a sibling skill instead of drafting the messages

evals.prompt: Tandrel has two SDRs and we enroll 900 active prospects per launch. The cadence we drafted is 9 touches over 18 working days: 5 automated emails and 4 manual steps (two calls with voicemail, two LinkedIn touches). We send from two mailboxes, both registered about three weeks ago on a fresh domain we bought for outbound. Leadership wants this live Monday. Does this hold up, and if it doesn't, what do we change?
evals.expected_output: Explicit capacity arithmetic showing roughly 100 manual touches per rep per day and roughly 125 sends per mailbox per day, both over the limits, the warm-up problem on the three-week-old domain flagged, and the fix bought in the ranked order starting with staggered cohort entry.
expectations: Computes manual-touch load as active prospects times manual touches divided by sequence length in working days, then divided across the two reps, landing near 100 manual touches per rep per day
States that roughly 100 manual touches per rep per day is far beyond a realistic daily call block, citing practitioner ranges of roughly 10-30 dials plus social touches
Computes automated sends as active prospects times automated touches divided by working days divided by mailboxes, landing near 125 sends per mailbox per day
Flags that this exceeds the practitioner ceiling of well under 100 cold sends per mailbox per day
Flags that both mailboxes are about three weeks old and still need a warm-up ramp measured in weeks before full volume
Recommends staggering cohort entry into daily batches as the first fix, ahead of every other option
Ranks cutting the active cohort above dropping a manual touch, because cutting the cohort keeps the design comparable to the previous cohort while dropping a touch forfeits that comparison
Ranks adding mailboxes or reps last and names its cost as a quarter to hire or weeks of warm-up ramp
Refuses to short-circuit the warm-up ramp by pushing the new domain to full volume for the Monday deadline
Warns that manual steps silently skipped by overloaded reps corrupt the measurement, because the sequence run is no longer the sequence designed
Hands the domain authentication, warm-up execution, and placement audit to the deliverability sibling skill rather than performing it inline
States the spam-complaint ceiling as below 0.3% with below 0.1% recommended, and identifies it as mailbox-provider platform policy rather than a vendor benchmark

evals.prompt: Nuvela is a DTC skincare brand, about 14,000 sessions a month and a 68% cart abandonment rate. Here's the flow I want built: SMS at 1 hour, email at 2 hours with 15% off, second SMS at 6 hours, email at 24 hours bumping to 20% off, then a final SMS at 48 hours. We capture everyone's mobile number at checkout so we have all the numbers already. These people are also on our weekly newsletter list, which I assume is fine since it's a different channel. Build it out.
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt abandonment flow gated on express SMS opt-in, capped at one SMS inside quiet hours, with no discount on touch 1, the incentive moved to +24-48h, cross-flow suppression from the newsletter, a global frequency cap, and immediate exits.
expectations: Refuses SMS to mobile numbers captured at checkout without express marketing opt-in, and frames it as a consent basis question rather than a design tradeoff
Caps the flow at a single SMS, and only for subscribers with express opt-in
Requires the SMS to land inside the jurisdiction's quiet hours and says to confirm the jurisdiction's rules rather than assume a window
Places touch 1 a few hours after abandonment with no discount
States that discounting touch 1 trains abandonment
Places the incentive on the second touch at roughly plus 24 to 48 hours
Ends the flow after the final touch rather than continuing indefinitely
Requires one active flow at a time per person
Suppresses subscribers who are in this flow from the weekly batch newsletter
States a global frequency cap across all marketing sends per subscriber
Makes exits on purchase, reply, or opt-out immediate, the same as B2B reply exits
States the consent basis per channel before designing the flow

evals.prompt: Kessline is six weeks into a 7-touch outbound sequence for our 400-prospect list. Open rate is 61%, which the team is thrilled about. But sequence completion rate is only 22% - most prospects never reach touch 7 - so I want to set an 80% completion target for the quarter and hold reps to it. Separately, touch 1 came back with 1.1% replies after four days and I'm ready to kill the whole thing and rebuild. Our CRM doesn't write meetings back to sequences so we can't see meetings per sequence, but the sequencer reports replies fine. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Open rate rejected as inflated and non-decisive, completion rate refused as a target and reframed as diagnostic, the touch-1 kill decision refused, reply rate committed as the decision metric with a numeric threshold and a post-cohort review date, and one variable per revision.
expectations: States that open rate is not a decision metric because mail-privacy proxies register phantom opens, and calls the 61% figure inflated
Refuses sequence completion rate as a team target and calls it diagnostic only
Explains that completion rate is a function of the sequence's own length and exit rules, so it means nothing against a borrowed or imposed threshold
Notes that a low completion rate partly reflects prospects exiting on reply, which is the sequence working rather than failing
Refuses to judge or kill the sequence on touch-1 data
States that most replies arrive after the first touch and labels that as vendor-published
Commits reply rate as the decision metric because meetings per 100 prospects is not measurable with this CRM setup
Names the measurement order: reply rate, then positive-reply rate, then meetings per 100 prospects, then connect rate, then completion rate
Places opt-out rate and spam-complaint rate outside that ranking as guardrails rather than goals
Gives a numeric cumulative reply-rate threshold and labels borrowed calibration figures as vendor-published
Evaluates at sequence level after a full cohort completes rather than mid-flight
Changes exactly one variable in the revision rather than rebuilding length, copy, and list at once

evals.prompt: Orrowind has 1,840 closed-lost opportunities from the last 18 months sitting in the CRM. Our VP wants a Q4 win-back blast to all 1,840 - four emails over two weeks - and then wants to re-run the same blast every quarter so the list stays warm. Two wrinkles I noticed: about 340 of those contacts currently have an open opportunity with a different rep, and roughly 90 of them got our breakup email during the original sequence. Put the plan together.
evals.expected_output: A trigger-gated re-engagement plan replacing the quarterly calendar blast, scoped to the small fraction of the list with a fresh trigger, with the 340 open-opp and 90 breakup contacts suppressed, a two-cycle re-entry cap, and an explicit nurture-or-sunset decision.
expectations: Gates re-entry on a fresh trigger such as a job change, funding, or tech-stack change, never on the calendar alone
Rejects re-enrolling the whole 1,840-record list
States that only a small fraction of a stale list develops a fresh trigger in any given quarter, and targets that fraction
Defines stale as roughly 90-180 days without engagement and labels that a practitioner range
Recommends a short 2-3 touch sequence that leads with the trigger rather than the proposed four-email blast
Suppresses the 340 contacts with an open opportunity before enrollment
Suppresses the roughly 90 contacts who already received a breakup email until a genuine new trigger appears for them
Caps re-entries at two cycles
After two cycles, forces a single explicit choice between long-term nurture and sunset rather than defaulting to nurture
Conditions long-term nurture on the account still fitting the ICP and on a named owner maintaining the list
Warns that defaulting to nurture on a list nobody maintains parks a dead cohort against the sending domain
Requires verifying each re-entry trigger before re-enrolling, or asking the user to confirm it

evals.prompt: Halterway sells warehouse labor-scheduling software to mid-market 3PLs. Each of our two SDRs works about 180 accounts and both already run a daily call block. Our sending domain is two years old with a clean record. Here's the channel plan we drafted: every prospect gets a personalized LinkedIn connection note referencing their most recent post - we budget 6 minutes per prospect for that - plus a Loom video on day 2, a text message on day 5 since we have mobile numbers from our data provider, and three emails spread across the rest. What order should we build these in, and is anything missing?
evals.expected_output: The channel efficiency order stated outright, personalized connection notes and unconsented SMS deleted rather than demoted, video pushed to last and restricted, an in-thread bump added, and the call block promoted with what the ranking starves named.
expectations: States the channel order explicitly as in-thread bump, then blank connection request, then extra email angle, then call plus voicemail, then social DM, then video message
Deletes personalized connection-request notes rather than ranking them lower, and states that blank requests connect as well as or better with identical downstream reply rates
Reclaims the 6 minutes per prospect that the personalized note was costing
Deletes SMS to prospects who have not given express opt-in, on the grounds that there is no consent basis, rather than ranking it as a weaker option
Ranks the video message last and names it the heaviest per touch and the one that never templates
Restricts video to a named-account list small enough for an SDR to hold in their head
Adds an in-thread bump and identifies it as near-zero cost on every axis
States that email carries the ask and every other channel exists to lift email replies
Notes that the warm two-year-old domain gives email headroom and therefore promotes email touches rather than forcing the call block
Keeps the call block in the plan given the two staffed SDRs, and names that a pure efficiency ranking starves the human-voice channels
Restricts social DMs to after the connection is accepted, at most two, with no pitch, phased out mid-sequence
Says out loud which channels were dropped and why when presenting the plan
Labels the channel ordering as practitioner guidance rather than law

evals.prompt: Quennard just exhibited at a logistics trade show and we came home with 212 badge scans. Sales wants to hit them hard while it's fresh: day 1 gets an email plus a call plus a voicemail plus a LinkedIn DM plus a connection request, day 2 gets another email plus a call, day 3 gets an email plus a DM, then a daily email for the following week. They also want the day-1 emails to fire at 6am local so we're sitting at the top of the inbox when people open their phones. Our scans are split roughly half US, a quarter Germany, a quarter Japan. Write the plan.
evals.expected_output: The pile-up rejected and rebuilt as a 3-4 touch event follow-up over 7-10 days with the first touch inside 48 hours, at most one labeled cluster day, widening gaps, recipient-local business-hour sends across the three geographies with holidays skipped, and the cost of the proposed plan named.
expectations: Rejects the proposed day-1, day-2, day-3 stacking as a same-day multi-channel pile-up
Allows at most one intentional, explicitly labeled multi-channel cluster day in the plan
Keeps every other day to no more than two channels
Widens gaps toward the tail instead of sending a daily email for the following week
Recommends an event follow-up shape of roughly 3-4 touches over 7-10 days
Places the first touch within 48 hours of the event while memory is fresh
States that the event follow-up shape is a convention across comparable playbooks rather than measured data
Rejects the 6am send and schedules touches inside recipient-local business hours
Skips holidays for each of the US, German, and Japanese segments rather than using one calendar
Warns that the proposed plan spends the whole channel budget before any reply data arrives and leaves nothing for week 2
Names opt-outs and spam complaints damaging the sending domain for every other sequence as a cost of the pile-up
Lists the immediate-exit conditions and a pre-enrollment suppression step for the scanned list
